Problem 275. Reading a layered map legend (A1)
A map legend translates symbols into properties. One location may have several properties at the same time.

Legend: tree=forest, wavy line=river, double line=road, arch=bridge, square=village, triangle=hill. Cells: A1 has forest, road; A2 has bridge, river; B1 has bridge, forest, river, road; B2 has road, village. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 11 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

A cell satisfies the task only if it has every required attribute. Extra attributes do not disqualify it unless the task says so. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.
Which cell or cells satisfy all of these conditions: river, road? Explain by intersecting the clues. Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

1. Convert the requested symbols into the attribute set ['river', 'road']. 2. Check each cell for every required attribute. 3. The matching set is ['B1']. Cross-domain check: 11−4=7 independent reports remain.

Problem 276. Choosing a safe settlement site: case 1
Human settlements depend on several factors at once. Some conditions may be compulsory while others are preferences.

Candidate sites: Site A: water=yes, road=yes, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=2; Site B: water=yes, road=no, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=4; Site C: water=yes, road=yes, flood-zone=yes, nearby farmland score=4; Site D: water=no, road=yes, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=6. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 5 cm apart.

A valid site must have water, road access, and must not be in the flood zone. Among valid sites, choose the one with the highest farmland score. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.
Which site should be selected under the stated mandatory conditions and preference rule? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

1. Separate mandatory conditions from the preference. 2. Filtering by water, road, and flood safety leaves ['Site A']. 3. Compare only the farmland scores of feasible sites: Site A=2. 4. Site A has the best score among valid sites. Cross-domain check: 5×3=15 km.
Good decisions first satisfy hard constraints and only then optimize among the remaining options.
Constraint-satisfaction problem followed by a score maximization over feasible options.
Problem 277. Choosing a safe settlement site: case 2
Human settlements depend on several factors at once. Some conditions may be compulsory while others are preferences.

Candidate sites: Site A: water=yes, road=yes, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=3; Site B: water=yes, road=no, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=3; Site C: water=yes, road=yes, flood-zone=yes, nearby farmland score=5; Site D: water=no, road=yes, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=5. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 12:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break. Mixed-domain verification: a regional archive has 29 map sheets and receives 8 additional sheets during the exercise.

A valid site must have water, road access, and must not be in the flood zone. Among valid sites, choose the one with the highest farmland score. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration. For this verification, the final number of sheets equals starting sheets plus received sheets.
